title: You can keep billing 2026 maternity codes until the end of 2027, if your payer lets you
summary: On 30 October, HHS published a guidance letter allowing HIPAA covered entities to use CPT 2026 maternity codes between 1 January and 31 December 2027, for pregnancies that start in 2026 and end in 2027. Read the next sentence carefully, because payers may issue business rules under it. May, not must. It does not let you keep using the old codes. It lets your payers decide whether you can.
body_markdown:
## HHS answered the cross-year question on 30 October


On 30 October, nine days before the CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule went on public inspection, HHS published a[Statement of Enforcement Discretion](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/cms-enforcement-discretion-maternity-care-services-cpt-guidance-letter-508.pdf) on maternity coding.


The publication answers the question of what happens to a pregnancy that starts in 2026 and ends in 2027.


> The Office of Health Technology & Products (OHTP), Standards & Interoperability Group (SIG) on behalf of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), announces an enforcement discretion under 45 CFR 162.1101 allowing HIPAA covered entities to temporarily use CPT 2026 Maternity Care Services codes for billing and payment purposes between January 1, 2027, and December 31, 2027.


This creates a full year long window.


## A careful read


> Effective Immediately: Under this temporary flexibility, payers and health plans **may** issue business rules in advance of January 1, 2027, instructing providers, clearinghouses and other trading partners regarding CPT code use when billing for Maternal Care Service episodes of care in which services begin in 2026 and end in 2027.


**May.** Not must.


The way we read this is, payers now have latitude to enable practices to bill using 2026 codes. What HHS commits to is narrow and conditional:


> Effective January 1, 2027: HHS will refrain from taking HIPAA Administrative Enforcement action against HIPAA covered entities that abide by payer and health plan business rules issued secondary to this temporary enforcement discretion.


So the protection attaches to following a payer's rule, not to using the old codes on your own judgement.


The letter also sets expectations for what those rules should look like. They should


> minimize disruptions for providers, result in accurate payment for providers, align with guidance issued by the American Medical Association regarding the use of its restructured 2027 CPT Maternity Care Services codes, and be phased out as soon as operationally feasible in 2027.


"Phased out as soon as operationally feasible" is worth noting. The window closes 31 December 2027, and HHS is signalling it would rather you did not use all of it.


## What this changes for you on Monday


**You now have something specific to ask every payer.** Not "what are you doing about 2027," which has produced vague answers all year, but: have you issued a business rule under the 30 October HHS enforcement discretion, and what does it say? That is a yes or no question about a named document.


**The answer may differ by payer** , because the letter leaves it to each of them.


**Silence is not permission.** A payer that has issued nothing has left you on the 2027 codes from 1 January for every date of service, regardless of when the pregnancy started.


## Separately: CMS declined to create the G-codes


In the same week, the CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule settled the other open question. CMS had solicited comment on creating 15 HCPCS G-codes that would have preserved the old global maternity structure for Medicare. It decided against:


> After consideration of public comments, we are not finalizing the creation of these HCPCS G-codes, although we may consider the creation of bundled codes describing maternity care services in future rulemaking.


CMS reports that almost all commenters opposed them, on the grounds that a Medicare-only code set would add administrative burden and market confusion. On the new CPT structure, CMS was brief: "After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing as proposed."


**This resolves payers like**[Wellpoint New Jersey,](https://providernews.wellpoint.com/nj/articles/reimbursement-policy-update-maternity-services-coding-change-32523) who planned to adopt the G-codes if they were finalized.


**Cigna** said it was waiting on the same rule and told providers not to move early. It now has roughly seven weeks to publish and operationalise. We will post its notice when it lands.


## One payment detail worth knowing


CMS did not simply accept the RUC's valuations. It removed four prenatal E/M visits from the utilization assumption and moved those RVUs into labor and delivery, on the reasoning that ACOG's 2025 guidelines make 12 prenatal visits no longer typical.


The result is roughly a 15 percent increase in work RVUs for each labor and delivery code against the RUC recommendation. Primary cesarean delivery goes from a recommended 12.00 to 13.80. Repeat cesarean from 14.66 to 16.86.


CMS was explicit that this is not clinical guidance: "we are not endorsing a reduced number of prenatal visits for pregnant women."


## What does not change


The payers that already moved are unaffected. They transitioned under the CPT structure, which is the structure that now stands.


- **Aetna** moved 1 September 2026, keyed to how many prenatal visits a patient had in 2026.
- **Highmark** moved 1 October 2026, keyed to the patient's due date.


Of the 181 health plans we have confirmed are moving off global maternity billing, 127 named a date and 96 of those dates have already passed.


## The group to watch now


54 plans have confirmed they are transitioning and never named a date. Everything they could reasonably have been waiting for has now happened, which makes the next few weeks the likeliest window for them to publish.


A plan that publishes in mid December and expects compliance on 1 January gives you three weeks. Those are the notices worth watching for.


## Where this comes from


We track over 3000 health plans and read their maternity policies as they publish. Every provider organization we could find that delivers babies has a public page listing its payers, what each has published, the effective date, and a link to the source. Free, no form, no sign-up.
